metaDescription: Practical 2026 guide to visiting Türkiye during Ramadan: official dates, what stays open in Istanbul, Bodrum, and Konya, iftar dinners, and etiquette.
quickAnswer: Visiting Türkiye during Ramadan is straightforward and rewarding for international travellers. Under the [official Diyanet calendar](https://vakithesaplama.diyanet.gov.tr/dinigunler.php?yil=2026), Ramadan 2026 runs from February 19 to March 19, followed by Ramazan Bayramı on March 20–22. Museums, sights, and most restaurants and bars in Istanbul and coastal resorts stay open, while evenings come alive with iftar tables.

body.text: Are restaurants, bars and sights open during Ramadan in Türkiye?

Yes—almost all museums, archaeological sites, hotels, restaurants, and bars in Istanbul, Cappadocia, and along the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts operate normally throughout Ramadan. Türkiye is a secular republic with no legal ban on daytime eating or alcohol sales, though some small neighbourhood eateries in conservative districts close until sunset.

During the 29 days of fasting (February 19 to March 19, 2026, per [Diyanet's official religious calendar](https://vakithesaplama.diyanet.gov.tr/dinigunler.php?yil=2026)), major sights follow standard seasonal hours. The real scheduling disruption happens during Ramazan Bayramı (Eid al-Fitr, March 20–22, 2026), when state museums often open later on the first morning, banks and post offices close, and domestic holidaymakers pack highways and flights.

Because Ramadan in 2026 falls in late winter and early spring, daytime sightseeing pairs well with off-peak hotel rates—see our [Türkiye in winter travel guide](https://itineraryofturkiye.com/blog/turkey-in-winter-premium-travel-guide) for cold-weather pacing tips.
How does the atmosphere differ between Istanbul, Bodrum and Konya?

The Ramadan experience varies dramatically by city and even by neighbourhood. Coastal Bodrum feels almost unchanged during the day, Istanbul splits between lively secular quarters and festive historic districts, and conservative Anatolian cities like Konya grow noticeably quieter until sunset transforms their squares after the evening call to prayer.

body.text: What is an iftar dinner experience like for visitors?

An iftar dinner is one of Türkiye's warmest culinary traditions, and non-Muslim visitors are genuinely welcome to join restaurant set menus or public square gatherings. Recognised on the [UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list](https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/iftar-eftari-iftar-iftor-and-its-socio-cultural-traditions-01984), iftar begins at sunset with dates, olives, and warm Ramazan pidesi before moving into soup and slow-cooked mains.

Around 45 minutes before sunset, bakery queues stretch down residential streets for sesame-topped Ramazan pidesi, baked exclusively during this month, as highlighted in [GoTürkiye's Ramadan guide](https://goturkiye.com/halaltourism/ramadan-and-ramadan-feasts). Traffic peaks sharply right before the sunset call to prayer, then empties within minutes.

If you plan to dine out around sunset, book your table a day ahead—many traditional Turkish restaurants switch to fixed multi-course iftar menus between 18:00 and 20:30, finishing with rosewater-scented güllaç and spiced Osmanlı şerbeti (Ottoman sherbet). Later in the night, you may still hear the Ramazan davulcusu (pre-dawn drummers) waking neighbourhoods for sahur, a custom documented by [Turkish Airlines' cultural guide](https://blog.turkishairlines.com/en/ramadan-in-turkiye-culture-and-traditions/).
What respectful etiquette should travellers keep in mind?

You do not need to fast as a visitor, and locals never expect tourists to follow religious observances. Simple situational awareness—avoiding eating or smoking directly outside mosques in conservative areas and allowing extra travel time before sunset—goes a long way toward smooth, respectful travel.
Keep these practical habits in mind:

items: Be discreet in conservative districts: In Fatih, Eyüp, Konya, or Şanlıurfa, eat inside cafés rather than walking down the street with takeaway food or cigarettes during daylight hours.
Avoid booking dinner right at sunset without a reservation: Kitchens focus on synchronized iftar service; dine before 17:30 or after 20:30 if you prefer à la carte ordering.
Expect pre-iftar traffic gridlock: In Istanbul, taxis and bridges stall 60 to 90 minutes before sunset as commuters race home; use ferries or the metro instead.
Check mosque prayer closures: Mosques stay busy for evening teravih prayers, so schedule interior visits for mid-morning or early afternoon.
Book early for Ramazan Bayramı: Lock in domestic flights and coastal rooms well ahead of March 20–22, 2026.

faq.q: When is Ramadan in Türkiye in 2026?
faq.a: According to Diyanet, Türkiye's Presidency of Religious Affairs, Ramadan 2026 begins on Thursday, February 19, 2026, and ends on Thursday, March 19, 2026, followed by the three-day Ramazan Bayramı holiday from March 20 to March 22, 2026.

faq.q: Can tourists drink alcohol during Ramadan in Türkiye?
faq.a: Yes. Bars, wine bars, meyhanes, and licensed hotel restaurants remain open in Istanbul's secular districts (Beyoğlu, Karaköy, Kadıköy, Beşiktaş), Cappadocia, and coastal resorts, though some traditional restaurants pause alcohol service during iftar.

faq.q: Are Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque open during Ramadan?
faq.a: Yes. Both remain open to visitors outside daily prayer times, though evening teravih prayers draw larger crowds. Visit between 09:00 and 11:30 for the calmest entry.

faq.q: Should I avoid visiting Türkiye during Ramazan Bayramı?
faq.a: You do not need to avoid it, but you must plan ahead. Expect busy highways, higher coastal hotel rates, and delayed first-morning museum openings from March 20 to March 22, 2026.

faq.q: Can non-Muslims book an iftar dinner at a Turkish restaurant?
faq.a: Yes. Most Ottoman and Turkish restaurants welcome all guests to their fixed-price iftar menus. Reserve in advance and arrive 15 minutes before sunset so the first courses land on time.

faq.q: What is the best seasonal food to try during Ramadan in Türkiye?
faq.a: Look for fresh sesame Ramazan pidesi straight from a neighbourhood bakery and güllaç, a delicate milk-and-rosewater pastry layered with walnuts and pomegranate seeds that rarely appears outside Ramadan.
